<reason>A wins the central analytical clash: B never showed what residency *duration itself* adds to safety beyond the supervision A explicitly retains ("a person can sit in-country for a decade without touching a seismic code" went unanswered). B's strongest move — the B2.1 claim that A's bridging/probation safeguards ARE residency — collapsed when A's Q1 exposed it as unfalsifiable and B4.1 doubled down "by definition," letting A5.2 land "defended a dictionary, not a policy." B kept defending supervised practice (which A incorporates) rather than residency-recognition per se, drifting from the motion's actual comparison. A also won the fairness clash (B never rebutted that the residency door selects for relocation wealth) and the verifiability clash narrowly (registry delisting as scalable containment vs. "no registry from which to delist a lying landlord"). B's residual live points — supervisor capacity/flooding, after-the-harm delisting, remote-work jurisdiction — were real but asserted rather than mechanized, and B partially misdescribed A's model (day-one probation, not "entitlement before anyone watches"). Both sides were disciplined, format-compliant (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure), and rhetorically strong; A simply resolved more of the live clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The definitional exchange over A's "credential as door, supervision as lock": B2.1's "the concession decides this round" was initially dangerous, but A's Q1 ("what pathway would ever not count?") plus B4.1's "by definition" answer confirmed the all-swallowing definitional trap, and A5.2's "defended a dictionary, not a policy" converted B's best attack into A's clearest win. Runner-up: A2.3's point that residency never directly tests local codes while bridging requirements do — the analytical gap B never closed.</best_rebuttal>
